document_meta.title: Rhode Island 2020 State Forest Action Plan

orientation.summary: This is the Rhode Island 2020 State Forest Action Plan (SFAP), a federally-required statewide forest planning document produced by the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (RIDEM) Division of Forest Environment. The document has a broad posture toward climate change, treating it as a significant stressor on forest health, composition, and management. It engages with range shift science primarily in discussing how climate change will alter species distributions — shifting suitable habitat for tree species and facilitating range expansion of southern species into Rhode Island — and how fragmentation impedes natural species migration. The document performs its own narrative synthesis drawing on external analyses (notably the New England Climate Change Response Framework vulnerability assessment) rather than applying its own quantitative models; it references external tools, publications, and projections but does not conduct original vulnerability, niche, or connectivity modeling. Actions described include promoting 'assisted migration' of tree species as a stated future goal, maintaining connectivity for wildlife, and priority landscape identification for conservation programs.

evidence_index.text: Climate change -increasing disturbances, alterations in species distributions and relationships, and compounding forest health threats
Rhode Island is already experiencing the impacts of climate change in the form of increasing temperatures, rising sea levels, and more intense rain and flood events.
As reported in Resilient Rhody, temperatures in Rhode Island have increased more than 3 degrees since the beginning of the 20th century, and sea level has risen 10 inches since 1930.
As the climate changes, forest composition will change, becoming less favorable to species that are adapted to cold climates, promoting typically southern species at the northern edge of their range

Increased temperatures and altered climate conditions are also expected to shift suitable growing conditions for individual species of trees, shrubs, and plants. This means that many species growing at their more southerly extent in Rhode Island may be unable to withstand the changes in growing conditions and become locally less common or disappear entirely. Meanwhile, species growing at their more northerly extent may find growing conditions conducive to expanding their range northward.

The natural shift in growing range and dispersal is a slow process but, in the 21 st century, it is complicated by grey infrastructure, permanent land conversion, and other impacts of fragmentation and forest loss which impede species migration.
The New England and Northern New York Forest Ecosystem Vulnerability Assessment and Synthesis presents an assessment of vulnerability for forest ecosystems for the end of the 21 st century

Although many of the common forest types across Rhode Island are generally expected to have some capacity to adapt to changing conditions, the likely effects of climate change also need to be considered at the property-and stand-levels where local site conditions and potential hazards can be evaluated.

Such shifts are expected to ultimately impact forest management decisions. The New England and Northern New York Forest Ecosystem Vulnerability Assessment and Synthesis presents an assessment of vulnerability for forest ecosystems for the end of the 21 st century, shown in the table below.

the combined onslaught of climate change, fragmentation and parcelization, interference with migration, loss of biodiversity, invasive plant and insect species, overuse and overgrazing, and more extreme weather events occurring more frequently -all contribute to forest lands with less biological resilience to change and less time to adapt to those changes.

Given enough time, forests and the species that rely on and support forests can adapt. But today, the combined onslaught of climate change, fragmentation and parcelization, interference with migration, loss of biodiversity, invasive plant and insect species
These increasing threats and rapid rate of change have the potential to exceed an ecosystem's resilience or capacity to adapt.

Warmer winters with fewer periods of sustained cold weather may lead to increased activity of forest insects and pests that have the potential to cause greater impacts to forests, as well as migration of more southerly pests as conditions become more favorable
Changes in the timing of leaf-out, flowering, and fruiting in plants can be very disruptive to plant pollinators, seed dispersers, and migratory wildlife.
longer growing seasons can mean desynchronized pollinators and food sources, bird nesting, and migration, etc., which may have unforeseen impacts.

Increasing winter temperatures also increase the threat from many invasive plants and insect pests (native and exotic) because these species may no longer have to withstand or recover from extremely cold winter conditions. A warmer climate may facilitate the establishment or increase the competitiveness of these threats

Expected consequences include increased activity of insect pests and diseases and higher infestation levels; more extreme exposure to heat waves and drought; and phenological mismatches with pollinators and dispersal agents.
Not only will warming temperatures provide conditions conducive for SPB outbreak, but they may also contribute to chronic stress factors to Rhode Island's pitch pine

Changes in seasonal weather patterns and precipitation amounts will have the greatest impact on the periodicity of outbreak occurrence. Cool April temperatures and sufficient precipitation to support the life cycle of Entomophaga maimaiga, a fungus that kills gypsy moth caterpillars, are necessary to maintain gypsy moth at low population levels.
More recently, changes in seasonal weather patterns and precipitation have decreased moisture availability in the summer months, increasing tree mortality.

One method is to encourage the planting of a variety of forest tree species that will be suited to the changing climate patterns. This can assist the migration of such species, avoiding interruptions caused by fragmentation and development, and speeding up the very slow movement of trees beyond their existing ranges.

DFE will also need to explore funding and partnerships to initiate efforts that will benefit Rhode Island, based on good science, such as planting and protection of seedlings, assisted migration, demonstration sites, and financial assistance.

The development of demonstration sites for various practices, including management practices for deer browse or assisted species migration, sequential prescribed fire recovery sites, and habitat enhancement would be invaluable when communicating messaging regarding stewardship, forest health, fire management, and even urban forests.

As populations grow and demand continues to increase, the resulting subdivisions, roads, utility corridors, and transmission installations result in smaller and smaller parcels with less and less connectivity, impacting the movement and subsequent genetic diversity of plants and animals
Even with increasing fragmentation, retaining green corridors connecting these core sites can play a crucial role for the sustainability of wildlife populations.

Provide technical assistance to the DEM Land Acquisition Committee, supporting protection of critical forest habitat, particularly larger intact blocks of high value forests for multiple benefits including connectivity and protection of wildlife habitat, and reduction in forest fragmentation.

climate_vulnerability.absence_note: The document references climate exposure clearly (shifting growing conditions, temperature increases affecting species) and engages with adaptive capacity (forests/species' ability to adapt, resilience to change). However, it never uses the term 'adaptive capacity' technically in the IPCC sense, nor does it explicitly decompose vulnerability into the three-axis framework. The referenced New England vulnerability assessment is incorporated by reference (a table of forest type vulnerability ratings), which provides vulnerability analysis that shapes management decisions. Score is 2 (exposure + adaptive capacity referenced) rather than 3 because the adaptive capacity dimension is referenced only generally — there is no systematic treatment of specific components of adaptive capacity as drivers of vulnerability scores.

partnerships_and_funding.absence_note: The document describes many existing partnerships and substantial federal/state funding for forest management broadly (CFAA, NRCS grants, RCPP, etc.) and acknowledges funding gaps in DFE capacity. However, specific funding and active partnerships dedicated to range-shift-related work (assisted migration, climate connectivity, climate-driven range-shift facilitation) are framed as aspirational — 'DFE will also need to explore funding.' Some landscape restoration grants (INCREASING RESILIENCY IN SOUTHERN NEW ENGLAND OAK FORESTS) tangentially address climate resilience but are about oak forest health, not range-shift facilitation specifically. Score is 1.

targeted_range_shift_actions.absence_note: The document explicitly names 'assisted migration' as an action to be explored, and frames tree planting of climate-suitable species as facilitating range shift. These are direct manipulation actions motivated by climate-driven range shifts, even if aspirational in framing ('DFE will also need to explore'). Score is 1.

time_bound_and_monitoring.absence_note: The document contains a strategies matrix with objectives and strategies but without specific deadlines or time-bound milestones attached to individual climate-related actions. The five-year RCPP funding period is mentioned. Effectiveness monitoring as a principle is noted in some programs but is not systematically operationalized at the action level for climate-related range-shift actions. Score is 1 (some time-bound structure present, but not paired with effectiveness monitoring for range-shift actions).

evidence.text: It is necessary for DFE to advocate and support adaptive forest management practices that maintain a resilient forest able to withstand the effects of stress related to changing climate zones and pests and diseases (whether native or exotic).

evidence_of_efficacy.absence_note: The document provides rationale for actions (e.g., forests provide resilience, assisted migration can help species track climate) but does not present evidence from prior studies or case studies directly evaluating the efficacy of specific climate adaptation actions. Some ecological first-principles are invoked (tree planting of climate-suitable species will assist migration). The energy-saving trees survivability data provides limited operational evidence. Score is 1 — rationale outlined but no specific efficacy evidence for range-shift actions presented.
projects: INCREASING RESILIENCY IN SOUTHERN NEW ENGLAND OAK FORESTS — A multi-state Landscape Scale Restoration grant project (MA, RI, CT). The project aims to increase oak resilience through education and stewardship, but no efficacy data from prior implementation is presented; it is described as a new effort.

Energy-Saving Trees Program — A tree-planting program with Arbor Day Foundation. The document notes an initial survivability study showing 78% of trees were planted correctly and alive at one year, providing limited evidence of implementation success (planting survival), but not evidence for climate adaptation efficacy of the action.
